titre: Sheppard: a trial held in the middle of the press
accroche: Cleveland, 1954: some twenty reporters sit less than a yard from the jury. In 1966, the Supreme Court overturns Sam Sheppard's conviction.
contenu_vulgarise:
On July 4, 1954, in Bay Village, a suburb of Cleveland (Ohio), Marilyn Sheppard, who is pregnant, is beaten to death in the bedroom of the family home. Her husband, the physician Sam Sheppard, says he was sleeping on a couch, heard a cry, saw a “form” near the bed, was struck on the back of the neck and lost consciousness. According to the Supreme Court, the coroner is reported to have told his men that very morning: “Well, it is evident the doctor did this, so let's go get the confession out of him.” The opinion calls the remark undenied.

## A case played out in the newspapers

On July 20, a front-page editorial charges that somebody is “getting away with murder” and blames the failures of the investigation on, among other things, “a husband who ought to have been subjected instantly to the same third-degree to which any other person under similar circumstances is subjected.” The next day, another editorial summons the coroner to hold his inquest. It takes place on July 22 in a school gymnasium and is broadcast live. Sheppard is searched there in front of several hundred spectators. His lawyers are present but are not allowed to take part, and one of them is thrown out of the room.

The trial opens on October 18, 1954, two weeks before the general elections in which the prosecutor and the judge, Edward Blythin, are both candidates. Three Cleveland newspapers have published the names and addresses of the seventy-five prospective jurors: anonymous letters and telephone calls reach them before the hearing even begins. All the jurors but one admit to having read or heard about the case.

## Twenty reporters inside the courtroom

The courtroom measures 26 feet by 48, about eight meters by fifteen. The judge has a long table set up inside the bar, normally reserved for lawyers, for about twenty representatives of newspapers and news agencies, one end of which is less than three feet from the jury. Behind the bar, four rows of benches are assigned for the whole trial: radio and television in the front row, outside reporters in the second and third. Photographers are allowed to photograph the jurors in their box and in the deliberation room: during the trial, their pictures appear more than forty times in the Cleveland newspapers alone. Sam Sheppard is convicted in December 1954 of second-degree murder and sent to prison for life, according to Wikipedia.

## What the Court faults, and whom

On June 6, 1966, the Supreme Court, in an opinion by Justice Clark, overturns the conviction. It does not fault the press for having written: it states that the press cannot be barred from reporting what happens in the courtroom. It faults the judge for not having protected the trial. He could have limited the number of reporters, and kept them from being seated inside the bar. He could have protected the witnesses, whose statements the press published before the hearing, and controlled what the police, the coroner and the lawyers told the newspapers. He could finally have postponed the case or transferred it to another county, and sheltered the jury.

In the words of the opinion, due process requires that the accused receive a trial by an impartial jury “free from outside influences,” and reversals are mere palliatives: the remedy lies in preventing prejudice at its source.

The Court says nothing about Sheppard's guilt. The State had the option of retrying him: he is acquitted at his second trial, the same year, according to Wikipedia. Who, in a courtroom, decides what gets in?

repere.texte: On June 6, 1966, in Sheppard v. Maxwell, the U.S. Supreme Court (opinion of Justice Clark) notes that some twenty reporters were seated at a table set up inside the courtroom, less than three feet from the jury box, and overturns Sam Sheppard's conviction for an unfair trial.
repere.source: Sheppard v. Maxwell, 384 U.S. 333 (1966), U.S. Supreme Court, opinion of Justice Clark

carte.punch: Twenty reporters within three feet of the jury: Sam Sheppard's trial, in 1954.
carte.idee: In Cleveland in 1954, twenty reporters sit at a table inside the courtroom, next to the jury of a physician accused of murdering his wife. In 1966, the Supreme Court overturns the conviction: the judge was supposed to protect the trial.
carte.source_courte: Sheppard v. Maxwell, U.S. Supreme Court, 1966

quiz.question: On what does the Supreme Court mainly base its decision to overturn Sheppard's conviction?
choix: On the absence of any physical evidence linking Sheppard to his wife's murder
On the fact that the judge failed to protect the jury or control the courtroom against pressure from the press
On the judge's refusal to hear the witnesses called by the defense
On a ban on newspapers reporting on the hearings of a criminal trial
quiz.explication: The opinion faults the judge for not taking the measures that would have preserved a fair trial: limiting the press's presence, sequestering the jury, moving the case. The opinion rules neither on the evidence nor on the witnesses, and it states that the press cannot be barred from reporting what happens at the hearing.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the Supreme Court, what does the coroner tell his men on the morning of the murder?
choix: Sheppard is innocent, let's look elsewhere for the real culprit
Question no one before a lawyer arrives
It is evident that it's the doctor, let's go get a confession out of him
The press must not yet be informed of the case
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Supreme Court notes that the coroner is said to have told his men, on the very morning of the murder, that it was evident Sheppard was guilty and that they should get a confession out of him, a remark the opinion says was never denied.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does the coroner's inquest of July 22, 1954 unfold?
choix: It is held behind closed doors, with no reporters present
In a school gymnasium, broadcast live, where Sheppard is searched in public
It is canceled at the request of Sheppard's lawyers
It is limited to the written hearing of the investigators, without Sheppard
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The coroner's inquest takes place on July 22, 1954 in a school gymnasium and is broadcast live; Sheppard is searched there in front of several hundred spectators, his lawyers present but with no right to take part.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happens to Sam Sheppard after his conviction is overturned in 1966?
choix: He is released outright, with no new trial possible
He stays in prison for life, the reversal applying only to the sentence
He is retried and once again sentenced to life in prison
The State retries him, and he is acquitted the same year
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1966 opinion overturns the conviction but says nothing about Sheppard's guilt; the State uses its option to retry him, and he is acquitted at that second trial, the same year, according to Wikipedia.
